summary: Authentication is vulnerable to SQL injection, token forgery, and insecure password verification.

findings.title: Username is interpolated into SQL
findings.body: findUser concatenates attacker-controlled username directly into the query, allowing crafted input to alter the statement and potentially bypass authentication or access/modify database data.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query or prepared statement and pass username as a bound parameter.

findings.title: JWT signing secret is embedded in source
findings.body: Every deployment uses the exposed constant to sign tokens; anyone who obtains the source can forge valid authentication tokens for arbitrary user IDs.
findings.recommendation: Load a strong per-environment secret from protected configuration, fail startup when it is missing, and rotate the exposed key.

findings.title: Password is compared directly to stored value
findings.body: login compares the submitted password to user.password with a direct equality check, indicating passwords are authenticated without a password-hash verification function; a database disclosure can therefore expose reusable credentials if values are stored as expected by this code.
findings.recommendation: Store passwords using a suitable password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt and verify them with the library's constant-time comparison API.

findings.title: Missing-user path can throw
findings.body: login dereferences user.password without checking whether findUser returned a user, so an unknown username or empty query result can cause an exception instead of a controlled authentication failure.
findings.recommendation: Normalize the query result and return an authentication failure when no user exists before accessing user fields.

samples.summary: Authentication is vulnerable to SQL injection, token forgery, plaintext password comparison, and invalid-user crashes.

findings.title: Username enables SQL injection
findings.body: findUser concatenates attacker-controlled username directly into the SQL statement at lines 7-9. A crafted username can alter the query, bypass authentication, or access/modify database data depending on driver permissions.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query with username supplied as a bound parameter.

findings.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret permits token forgery
findings.body: The JWT secret is embedded in source code at line 4. Anyone who obtains the source or deployed artifact can sign arbitrary session tokens, and the same secret is likely reused across environments.
findings.recommendation: Load a strong secret from an environment-specific secret store, fail startup when absent, and rotate the exposed key.

findings.title: Passwords are compared directly without verification hashing
findings.body: login compares the supplied password directly with user.password at line 15, indicating passwords must be stored or exposed in directly comparable form. A database compromise would expose usable credentials; loose equality also permits coercion.
findings.recommendation: Store salted password hashes and verify them with a password-hashing library using strict, timing-safe verification.

findings.title: Unknown users cause login to throw
findings.body: login dereferences user.password without checking whether findUser returned a user. A normal login attempt for a nonexistent username can therefore raise an exception instead of returning an authentication failure, potentially producing 500 responses or denial-of-service noise.
findings.recommendation: Handle an absent user before dereferencing it and return the same generic failure used for an incorrect password.

samples.summary: Authentication is vulnerable to SQL injection, token forgery after secret disclosure, and insecure password verification.

findings.title: Username enables SQL injection
findings.body: findUser concatenates attacker-controlled username directly into the SQL statement at lines 7-9. A crafted username can alter the query, bypass authentication, or read and modify database data depending on database permissions.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query with username passed as a bound parameter.

findings.title: JWT signing secret is embedded in source
findings.body: The static signing key at line 4 is exposed to anyone who can read the source or built artifact. Disclosure permits forging valid authentication tokens for arbitrary user IDs, and every deployment shares the same compromised key.
findings.recommendation: Load a strong deployment-specific secret from a secret manager or required environment variable, fail startup if absent, and rotate the exposed key.

findings.title: Passwords are compared as plaintext
findings.body: login compares the supplied password directly with user.password, implying passwords are stored or otherwise handled as plaintext rather than verified against a password hash. A database disclosure would expose reusable credentials.
findings.recommendation: Store passwords using a password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt and verify them with the library's comparison function.

findings.title: Issued authentication tokens never expire
findings.body: jwt.sign is called without an expiration, so stolen tokens remain valid indefinitely unless the signing key is rotated.
findings.recommendation: Set a short explicit expiresIn value and implement an appropriate refresh or reauthentication flow.
